extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent prosecutors, and patent attorneys (practitioners evaluating or drafting claims for subject-matter eligibility)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and examples for performing US patent subject-matter eligibility analysis under the Alice/Mayo two-step framework, including special analyses for nature-based products (markedly different characteristics). Intended to show how to apply Steps 1, 2A, and 2B to real claim fact patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1: Statutory category
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim is directed to a statutory category (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether the claim elements as a whole satisfy a statutory category (examples: a system including a mobile device and a server qualifies as a machine; a series of steps qualifies as a process; compositions qualify as composition of matter). (Text examples: 'A system ... satisfies the requirements of a machine (Step 1: YES).' 'A series of steps ... satisfies the requirements of a process (Step 1: YES).')

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A: Is the claim directed to a judicial exception?
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze whether the claim is 'directed to' a judicial exception such as an abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon, or product of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for recitations of mathematical operations, mental processes, organizing human activity, or nature-based subject matter. Examples cited: mathematical operations like calculating pseudo-ranges/absolute time (treated as abstract ideas); managing a Bingo game or creating contractual relationships (organizing human activity / fundamental economic practices). Note the example language: 'The claim recites mathematical operations ... which the courts have considered to fall within the judicial exceptions ... directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: YES).' Also: 'This describes the creation of a contractual relationship ... which is a commercial arrangement ... abstract idea (Step 2A: YES).'

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B: Additional-elements / inventive-concept inquiry (significantly more)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim's additional elements, individually or in combination, amount to significantly more than the judicial exception itself (i.e., supply an inventive concept).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether claimed extra features impose meaningful limitations on the exception or merely recite conventional/ generic implementation. Consider the claim elements both individually and in combination. Examples: reciting a general-purpose CPU, memory, display, or network at a high level does not transform an abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter; by contrast, meaningful limitations that apply the mathematical operations to improve existing technology may provide 'significantly more.' The guidance uses explicit Step 2B yes/no determinations in each example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer/implementation recitations are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciting conventional computer components (CPU, memory, network, printer, input/output terminal, program) at a high level does not add significantly more to an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple examples show that simply adding 'a computer with a CPU and memory' or 'a computer network' and asserting they perform basic functions is 'mere instructions to implement the abstract idea on a computer' and fails Step 2B. (Examples: Bingo, buySAFE, Ultramercial, Digitech explanations — 'these generic computer components are claimed to perform their basic functions ... do not amount to significantly more').

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical operations / data manipulation as abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical techniques, processing, and manipulation of data (e.g., generating data using Fourier analysis, computing pseudo-ranges, combining data into a profile) are treated as abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that 'simply describe the concept of gathering and combining data by reciting steps of organizing information through mathematical relationships' are directed to abstract ideas (Digitech example; Benson analogy). Such claims require additional elements that add significantly more to be eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizing human activity and fundamental economic practices as abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite schemes for organizing human activity (e.g., managing a game, underwriting/guaranteeing transactions, exchanging advertising for content) are likely abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guidance equates concepts like managing Bingo, creating contractual relationships (underwriting/guaranty), and using advertising as currency with other abstract ideas (Bilski/Alice). Narrowing to particular types or parts of the transaction does not remove abstractness. (See Planet Bingo, buySAFE, Ultramercial analyses.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant pre-solution activity does not confer eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Activities that merely gather information, record events, or perform routine steps necessary to implement the idea are insignificant pre-solution activities and do not supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: accessing/updating an activity log, requiring a consumer request, restricting access, or recording transactions are characterized as 'insignificant pre-solution activity' and do not add significantly more to an abstract idea (Ultramercial example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningful limitations that improve technology can provide 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that meaningfully limit application of the judicial exception and apply it to improve a technological process or device can render a claim eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the combination of elements imposes meaningful limits and effects a technological improvement (example: the GPS example — the programmed CPU 'acts in concert' with specific mobile-device features to improve signal-acquisition sensitivity and extend usefulness into weak-signal environments, and to provide location information for display). The guidance states that such features, especially in combination, 'amount to significantly more than the judicial exception (Step 2B: YES).' Use these factual showings when present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different characteristics test for nature-based products
rubrics_metrics.description: For claims to nature-based products (compositions derived from natural products or combinations of naturally occurring substances), determine whether the claimed product has 'markedly different characteristics' from any naturally occurring counterpart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the claimed product (as a whole) to naturally occurring counterpart(s). If no natural counterpart exists for the combination, compare to individual components as they occur in nature. If the claimed combination exhibits markedly different properties (e.g., explosive property of gunpowder, slowed spoilage of juice, improved bioavailability due to formulation), it is not a 'product of nature' exception and is not directed to a judicial exception (Gunpowder, Pomelo juice, Amazonic acid examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Process claims focused on nature-based products must be analyzed as product claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A process claim that is materially indistinguishable from claiming the nature-based product itself should be treated as directed to a nature-based product and subjected to the markedly different characteristics analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a claim 'comprising providing a pomelo fruit' is considered focused on the pomelo fruit per se and thus is analyzed as a nature-based product. If the claimed fruit has no markedly different characteristics from the naturally occurring fruit, the claim is directed to an exception and is ineligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims focused on assemblies/combined components may avoid nature-based analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are focused on an assembly of components whose focus is the assembly rather than the nature-based component(s) need not be subjected to the 'markedly different characteristics' test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a fountain-style firework that claims the assembly of components (cardboard body compartments, ignition fuse, sparking composition, gunpowder) is analyzed as an assembly and is not directed to a nature-based product (Step 2A: NO) because the claim is focused on the assembly rather than the nature-based components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different characteristics can be structural, chemical, physical, or functional
rubrics_metrics.description: Markedly different characteristics may arise from changes in chemical structure, physical form, or properties as compared to a natural counterpart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: chemical derivatization (5-methyl amazonic acid), removal of functional groups (deoxyamazonic acid), formulation changes causing different release/bioavailability (core enveloped by natural polymeric layer causing colonic release), or addition of solubilizing agents to create stable aqueous compositions. These differences support finding 'markedly different characteristics.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims are analyzed under their broadest reasonable interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility analyses are performed according to the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guidance repeatedly states that claims are analyzed for eligibility 'in accordance with their broadest reasonable interpretation,' and examples apply that interpretive standard when comparing claims to natural counterparts or determining whether a process claim is effectively a product claim.
